findings.title: Database write in validator without error handling
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.should_block?` calls `record.save` without any rescue. It is invoked from `EmailValidator#validate_each`, which runs during `User#valid?` / `User#save`. If the save fails (e.g. DB connection blip, lock timeout, race causing a stale `match_count` that triggers a future validation), ActiveRecord raises and the user sees a generic 500 instead of a clean signup error. Validators should be side-effect free and idempotent; the counter increment belongs either in `update_all` (atomic, no exception on no-op) or in an `after_validation` / async job, not inside a validator that runs on every attribute check.

findings.title: Blocked-email lookup is case- and whitespace-sensitive
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first` performs a literal equality match, and `BlockedEmail` neither downcases nor strips the email on save. The rest of the codebase treats email as case-insensitive (`User.find_by_username_or_email` downcases via `Email.downcase`, `users_controller#change_email` strips and downcases). A user can trivially bypass a block by signing up with `BAD@spamclub.com`, `bad@spamclub.com ` (trailing space), etc., and the same bypass defeats the admin's intent when they later look up rows in `blocked_emails`. Normalize the email (downcase + strip) on both write (`before_validation`) and read inside `should_block?`.

findings.title: Lost-update race in match_count increment
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` is a read-modify-write on a single row with no row lock. Under any concurrent signups for the same blocked address (and Discourse runs Puma/clustered workers), two callers can both read e.g. `match_count = 5`, both bump to 6, and both persist 6 — losing one increment. The same problem affects `last_match_at`. Use an atomic SQL update, e.g. `BlockedEmail.where(id: record.id).update_all(["match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?", Time.zone.now])`, so the counter cannot be lost.

findings.title: Regex metacharacters in domain setting are not escaped
findings.body: `email_in_restriction_setting?` only does `setting.gsub('.', '\.')` before building `Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true)`. The whitelist/blacklist values are admin-controlled site settings that may contain `|`, `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `+`, `*`, `?`, `^`, `$`, `\`. A value like `gmail.com|mail.ru` would match `@gmail.com` *or* `@mail.ru` (the first `|` makes `mail.ru` a separate alternative of the whole group, not a literal). Also, because the pattern is `@(...)` with no anchors, a blacklist value of `mail.ru` already matches `user@mail.ru.example.com`. Escape all regex metacharacters and anchor the match (e.g. require the domain to end at a non-word character or end of string) so neither false positives nor ReDoS-via-admin-setting is possible.

findings.title: EmailValidator spec does not exercise whitelist/blacklist paths
findings.body: The spec only covers the `BlockedEmail.should_block?` branch via Mocha stubs. The whitelist and blacklist branches (the original purpose of `email_validator`, moved out of `User`) are completely untested. Without covering those, a regression that, say, swaps the `if`/`elsif` to make blacklist override whitelist, or one that breaks the regex escape, would pass tests. Add at least one case each for: (a) whitelist present, email not in whitelist -> error added, (b) whitelist present, email in whitelist -> no error, (c) blacklist present, email in blacklist -> error added, (d) blacklist present, email not in blacklist -> no error, and (e) error from whitelist suppresses the BlockedEmail branch.
